← Plantation shutter bid calculator

How much to charge to install plantation shutters

Window-treatment shops get shopped on a published $250 a window installed Facebook special. Those numbers cannot see the opening or the extras. Six 30×60 2-panel inside-mount paint-grade hangs are a different job from eight 48×80 4-panel outside-mount stain-grade openings on a second story with treatment removal and a bypass track.

Open the free plantation shutter bid calculator

Price the openings and the extras, not the $250 dump

A shutter install is openings, then a mount, then how much of that job is actually sold. Product-on-site hang is the cheap special: the shutters are already in the truck. Measure-and-install is a typical shop trip. Template-and-custom is a millwork path plus the hang. Inside mount is jamb and sill. Outside mount is trim, returns, and more hardware.

A hang-only special is not a template mill job

The cheap special is almost always six small inside-mount paint-grade openings, two panels each, no removal, no bypass. A stain-grade template house on a second story is a different crew week. Matching a per-opening number on a custom job is how a sold shutter becomes a loss when the millwork and the second story eat the margin.

This is not window replacement, window cleaning, or a patio door

Window replacement is glass, united inches, and a nailing flange. Window cleaning is panes. A patio door is sliders as an opening. Interior painting is a coat. This prices a shutter install: openings, mount, grade, and extras.

Walk-away price

Load the wage with payroll burden. Add overhead as a share of direct cost. Then take margin as a share of the customer’s price, not a markup on cost. The walk-away number is total cost. A proposed price under that number loses money before you take anything out of it.

This page is a walkthrough of the arithmetic in the plantation shutter bid calculator. It is not a window design, a building-code determination, a mill catalog, or a price you should copy onto a contract.

Common questions

How much should I charge to install plantation shutters?

Charge from openings, mount, grade, and extras — not a published $250-a-window special. Six 30×60 2-panel inside-mount paint-grade hangs are a different job from eight 48×80 4-panel outside-mount stain-grade openings on a second story with treatment removal and a bypass track.

Is a product-on-site hang the same bid as a template-and-custom job?

No. Product-on-site hang is the cheap special: the shutters are already in the truck. Measure-and-install is a typical shop trip. Template-and-custom is a millwork path plus the hang. Matching a per-window special on a custom house is how a sold job becomes a loss when the millwork and the second story eat the margin.

How do mount, grade, and extras change a shutter price?

Inside mount is jamb and sill. Outside mount is trim, returns, and more hardware. Paint-grade is the cheap-special assumption. Stain-grade is a different mill invoice. Treatment removal, a specialty shape, a bypass track, a café split, and a second story do not live in a published per-window special.

Is this the same as window replacement, window cleaning, or a patio door?

No. Window replacement is glass, united inches, and a nailing flange. Window cleaning is panes. A patio door is sliders as an opening. This prices a shutter install: openings, mount, grade, and extras.

vs-a-flat-per-window-special.html.text:
← Plantation Shutter Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat per-window special

"$250 a window installed" is not a price for a job — it is a price for six small inside-mount paint-grade openings hung from the truck, quietly reused for every house that also asks for plantation shutters.

What a flat per-window special is

A flat per-window special is the fastest way to quote a shutter job over the phone or on a Facebook ad: quote the published $250-a-window number, skip the walkthrough. Homeowners shop it because a flyer or a post already gave them a figure, and it is the figure they will ask you to match — even for a job the number was never priced on.

The number behind it was set for one kind of job — small inside-mount openings, paint-grade, hung straight from stock with nothing to remove — and then reused for every house afterward, whether or not the next one needs an outside mount, a stain-grade mill invoice, a measure-and-template trip, or a second story.

What this calculator is

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter the openings, the typical width and height, panels per opening, the mount (inside or outside), the grade (paint or stain), the scope (product-on-site hang, measure-and-install, or template-and-custom), and whether the job needs treatment removal, a specialty opening, a bypass track, or a cafe split, plus your own wage, payroll burden, overhead, and target margin. It returns the bid price, the price per opening, and the walk-away price below which the job loses money — for this mount and this grade, not a flat number for every house.

What a flat per-window special doesWhat this calculator does instead
Charges the same figure per window for an inside-mount paint-grade hang and an outside-mount stain-grade template job — even though the mill invoice and the hang hours on the second job can run several times the first. Prices the mount, the grade, and the scope separately, from panels per opening and square footage, not a blended per-window number.
Has no line for treatment removal, a specialty or arched opening, a bypass track, or a cafe split, regardless of whether the job the customer wants actually needs them. Prices each of those as its own labor and material line, applied only when the job calls for it.
Quotes the same rate for a one-story ranch and a second-story job that needs a ladder or scaffold on every opening. Prices extra stories as their own labor line, applied per opening above the ground floor.
Has no separate line for a measure trip or template-and-custom milling, which a stain-grade or unusual-opening job usually needs and a product-on-site hang does not. Prices measure and template hours separately by scope, so a millwork job is not priced like a hang-only job.
Gives the estimator a number to quote, not a number to check a quote against. Reports the walk-away price and the dollar gap against what a flat per-window special would have quoted the same job, so a shopped price can be scored against real cost before you commit to it.

Two houses, one flat special

Using this calculator's own shipped presets, at a $42 crew wage, 32% payroll burden, 15% overhead, and a 20% target margin — the form's own defaults, not a number invented for this page:

The cheap-special preset — 6 openings, 30×60, 2-panel, inside mount, paint-grade, hang only — walks away at $5,348.16 and this calculator bids it at $6,685.20 ($1,114.20 per opening). A flat $250-a-window quote on the same 6 openings comes to $1,500.00 — already $3,848.16 short of the job's own break-even cost.

Take the same $250-a-window rate to a template-and-custom job instead — 8 openings, 48×80, 4-panel, outside mount, stain-grade, two stories, a specialty opening, and a bypass track — and the job walks away at $20,943.86, with this calculator bidding it at $26,179.83 ($3,272.48 per opening). The same flat rate on 8 openings comes to $2,000.00 — $18,943.86 short of that job's own break-even cost, nearly five times worse than the cheap job's shortfall on the identical per-window rate. Same $250-a-window special, one house where it merely undercuts and one where it loses money on every opening the moment the mill invoice and the second story are counted.

Common questions

Why does a flat "$250 a window" special get a plantation shutter install wrong?

Because the cost driver is the mount, the grade, and the scope, not the panel in the truck. Six small inside-mount paint-grade openings hung straight from stock are a different job from eight wide outside-mount stain-grade openings on a second story that need a measure trip, custom milling, treatment removal, and a bypass track. A flat per-window special charges both the same because it was priced on the cheapest opening and mount combination, not the job in front of the estimator.

What does a flat per-window rate usually leave out entirely?

The mount, the grade, the scope, and the extras. A published $250-a-window number is set on an inside-mount, paint-grade, product-on-site hang -- it has no line for outside-mount trim and hardware, no line for a stain-grade mill invoice, no line for a measure trip or template-and-custom millwork, and no line for treatment removal, a specialty opening, a bypass track, a cafe split, or a second story.

How much do scope, mount, grade, and extras actually add over the per-window rate?

On this calculator's own shipped presets, at a $42 crew wage, 32% payroll burden, 15% overhead, and a 20% target margin -- the form's own defaults: the cheap-special preset -- 6 openings, 30x60, 2-panel, inside mount, paint-grade, hang only -- walks away at $5,348.16 against a flat $250-a-window quote of $1,500.00, already $3,848.16 short of its own break-even cost. The losing-job preset -- 8 openings, 48x80, 4-panel, outside mount, stain-grade, template-and-custom, two stories, a specialty opening, and a bypass track -- walks away at $20,943.86 against a flat quote of $2,000.00, $18,943.86 short of its own break-even cost -- nearly five times worse than the cheap job's shortfall on the same $250-a-window rate.

Is a flat per-window rate ever the right way to quote?

For a narrow band of similar jobs -- small inside-mount paint-grade openings hung straight from stock, no removal, no bypass, no second story -- a flat rate can land close, because that is probably the job the rate was set on. The risk is quoting an outside-mount stain-grade template job the same way sight unseen, because the rate does not know the mount, the grade, the scope, or which extras apply until someone counts the openings, and by then the flat number has often already been quoted.

Does this calculator know my local labor rates or material costs?

No. It has no data on your local labor market, your mill or hardware supplier's invoice pricing, or your shop's overhead. It takes the openings, the mount, the grade, the scope, and which extras apply, plus your own wage, burden, overhead, and target margin, and turns that into a price for this job -- the arithmetic a flat per-window special skips, not a market survey.

This calculator vs. Jobber

Two different shapes: Jobber is account-based field-service software for running a home-service business. This page is a free, private worksheet for one plantation shutter install before you quote it.

What each tool is for

Jobber is field-service management software founded in 2011 and headquartered in Edmonton, Alberta, Canada, used by home-service businesses across HVAC, plumbing, electrical, lawn care, and cleaning trades. It combines client management, quoting, scheduling, invoicing, and payment collection into one subscription system meant to run a whole business across every job and every crew, and it says it serves over 200,000 users. It is sold as an ongoing subscription account. Jobber's own pricing page is not reachable from this session to confirm today's exact plan names or dollar figures, so no price for it is invented here: only its well-documented identity and category — home-service field-service management software, sold as a subscription account — are stated, and no dollar amount for Jobber appears on this page.

This calculator does none of what Jobber does. It does not manage clients, schedule crews, send invoices, or collect payments, and it stores no customer or job record on a server. It takes the scope (product-on-site hang, measure-and-install, or template-and-custom), mount (inside or outside), finish (paint-grade or stain-grade), openings, panels, a second story, treatment removal, and a bypass track, and turns that into the walk-away price below which the job loses money, a copyable customer-facing bid summary, and a printable customer proposal with scope lines and a signature block.
